title: Oncall pocket runbook — API streaming & rate failures
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, operator-focused runbook for the most common API failure patterns we see in production: request timeouts, HTTP 429 spikes (rate-limiting/backpressure), degraded streaming (partial or choppy event streams), and generalized elevated error rates. It is intentionally concise for oncall use with quick checks, short mitigation actions, and escalation steps.

Context & assumptions:
- Applies to Hosted API endpoints and edge gateway. Dedicated/Private deployments may have different consoles but the triage logic is the same.
- Monitoring: Grafana dashboards for per-route latency, p99/p50, error-rate, downstream GPU availability; Kibana/ES for request traces and logs; Redis/kv and local cache metrics; API gateway (envoy/nginx) metrics.
- When in doubt, run the telemetry queries below first before changing config.

Quick triage checklist (first 5 minutes)
1) Confirm alert scope: is this single route, single model, region, or global? Check alert details and Grafana links.
2) Check global capacity signals: GPU-borrow/queue-depth, autoscaler events, node pool health.
3) Look at gateway 5xx vs runtime 5xx: is the gateway returning 429/timeouts or is the runtime failing?
4) For streaming issues, test a minimal streaming request (curl + stream) to see if chunks are emitted.
5) If customers are impacted, escalate to P1 flow and notify CS/Support for customer comms.

Essential telemetry queries (examples to run in Kibana/Logs):
- Recent 429s by route: index:api-requests | filter: status:429 | group by: route, host | last 15m
- Timeouts by request size: status:504 or timeout:true | group by: input_length_buckets | last 30m
- Streaming disconnects: filter: stream_disconnect:true | fields: route, client_ip, backend_error
- Error-rate heatmap: group by model_version, route, region | show 5xx and 4xx trends over last 1h

Quick mitigations (do in this order)
A. Soft rollback / fallback (fastest, safest)
- Switch traffic to a known-good model variant or previous model version via Console rollout UI (canary -> rollback). Use canary rollback button; pick the last stable version with green perf.
- If route-level config has an alternate non-streaming fallback, flip the route to the fallback mode (e.g., strict non-streaming text generation) to preserve availability.

B. Temporary rate-limits / emergency throttles
- In the Console, set emergency per-key throttle (reduce bucket to 10 req/min) or globally at the gateway to protect backends. Communicate to CS.
- If 429s are customer-visible because of sudden burst abuse, create a temporary exclusion/raise quota for paying customers only.

C. Circuit-breakers & batch sizing
- Toggle circuit-breaker to fail-fast on overloaded downstreams: console -> route -> advanced -> circuit_breaker = on. This reduces tail latency at expense of more 429s but prevents cascading queuing.
- Reduce max batch size on the model route to lower per-request latency if queue formation is causing timeouts.

D. Cache & prefix reuse check
- Check KV prefix cache hit ratio. If cache eviction is high and causing heavy model re-computation, increase cache retention for the hot prefix temporarily.

Concrete oncall play by failure mode
1) Timeouts (504 / client timeouts)
- Symptoms: rising p95/p99 latency; traces show requests stuck in runtime queue or GPU queue.
- Root checks: autoscaler events (scale up failed?), GPU memory OOMs, runtime log for lockups.
- Short-term: reduce batch size; enable fast-fail circuit-breaker; if available, switch to a lower-latency model variant (quantized / smaller).
- Longer-term (postmortem): investigate kernel selection changes, sequence length distribution shifts, and cold-cache patterns.

2) HTTP 429 spikes
- Symptoms: sudden increase in 429s across one or more routes, gateway metrics show rate limiting actions.
- Root checks: identify which layer produced 429 (gateway vs runtime vs model-serving layer). Check api-key-level usage and origin IPs for spikes.
- Short-term: increase gateway quota for critical customers, impose emergency throttles for unknown/unpaid keys, enable canary rollback of recent throttle rules.
- If 429s from runtime: examine queue depth, enable extra burst capacity (if Dedicated) or route to another region/model.

3) Degraded streaming (partial chunks, abrupt EOF)
- Symptoms: streams start, then stop emitting tokens; client sees partial outputs or hangs.
- Root checks: network flaps between gateway and runtime; keepalive timeout mismatches; chunk flush frequency settings in runtime.
- Short-term: toggle streaming batching to emit earlier (lower flush threshold), fall back to non-streaming response for impacted routes, or re-route to dedicated nodes with guaranteed low latency.
- If client-side issues suspected, ask CS for a sample request and reproduce with curl --no-buffer to confirm.

4) Elevated error rates (5xx, model runtime exceptions)
- Symptoms: rising 5xx across routes; logs show repeated same exception.
- Root checks: correlate with recent deploys (rollouts) — check rollout timeline in Console and PRs in runtime repo.
- Short-term: rollback the offending deployment, restrict traffic via canary weight 0, or remove optional features (tool-calling, function hooks) that surfaced the bug.

Emergency commands & useful snippets
- Reproduce a streaming request (local):
  curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -X POST
    -d '{"model":"gpt-x-small","input":"test","stream":true}'
    https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate
- Check queue depth (kubectl example, Dedicated):
  kubectl get hpa -n inference
- Quick log tail (Fluentd/Kibana):
  Kibana -> saved query: "route:<name> AND timestamp:now-15m..now"

Escalation & communication
- When to escalate to oncall-2: any of the following: sustained >5% user errors globally for >10m, tier1 customers impacted with SLAs breached, or inability to mitigate with soft rollbacks within 15m.
- Pager duty contact: oncall-2 (L2) -> eng-incident-lead -> SRE manager (in that order). If pager cannot be reached, use Slack #sre-oncall and mention @eng-leads.
- Customer communication starter: short note for CS with: impacted routes, estimated % requests failing, mitigation in flight (e.g., rollback to vX), ETA for full mitigation.

Short-term patch checklist (for post-incident status)
- Record the initial alert message and timeline of actions (who did what and when).
- Save representative request ids and traces (Kibana link) into the incident ticket.
- If rollbacks used, record the stable version and why it was chosen.
- Create follow-up tasks: re-evaluate autoscaler thresholds, add or tune alerting to avoid noisy 429 alerts, add a synthetic test for streaming chunk frequency.

Notes / operator reminders (raw, informal)
- TODO: add an explicit dashboard panel for "stream chunk latency" (we only have total latency now).
- Watch out for recent kernel/compilation PRs — they can affect tail latency even without errors.
- If you flip circuit-breaker, remember to disable it after capacity recovers; leaving it on can mask capacity issues for hours.
- If a customer reports degraded quality after fallback, escalate to product; do not re-enable broken model variant without signoff.

Post-incident template (paste into Jira/incident ticket)
- Incident summary: short sentence; scope (routes, customers); timeline (detection -> mitigation -> resolution).
- Root cause hypothesis: (short, one line).
- Actions taken: bullet list of rollbacks, throttles, toggles.
- Follow-ups: list of assigned tickets for improvements/tuning.
- Owner for postmortem: (name)

Appendix: quick references
- Console model rollouts: Console -> Models -> <model> -> Rollouts
- Gateway throttle controls: Console -> Network -> Rate Limits
- Circuit breaker toggle: Console -> Routes -> Advanced
- Useful logs: Kibana saved query "api-high-latency" and "api-429-spike"

Endnotes:
This is a living draft — add small actionable items here (concrete Grafana queries, exact Console button names) as you validate them oncall. If something is ambiguous here when you need it, make a one-line edit and push it back to this doc.
